title: AUD U3·W4 — Other Engagements: SSARS, Attestation & Governmental Auditing
lessonHtml:
Cold open — beyond the financial-statement audit

Not every CPA engagement is an audit. A practitioner may prepare, compile, or review statements; examine or perform agreed-upon procedures on other subject matter; or audit a government grant under GAGAS and the Single Audit. Each carries a different level of assurance, report, and independence rule. This final AUD week maps the engagement continuum — the knowledge that lets you pick the right service and the right report for MBG or any client.

The assurance continuum

Engagements differ chiefly in the assurance provided. An audit or examination gives reasonable (high) assurance and a positive opinion. A review gives limited (negative) assurance — "nothing came to our attention" — based mainly on inquiry and analytics. A compilation and a preparation give no assurance. Agreed-upon procedures give no assurance and no opinion — only findings the specified users evaluate themselves. The level of assurance drives the procedures, the report, and the fee.

SSARS engagements

The Statements on Standards for Accounting and Review Services (SSARS) govern non-audit work on a nonissuer's statements. A preparation engagement produces statements with no report and no assurance (a legend states no assurance is provided); independence is not required and need not be disclosed. A compilation adds a brief report but still no assurance and no procedures to verify; if the accountant is not independent, that fact is disclosed. A review provides limited assurance through inquiry and analytical procedures and requires independence; lack of independence precludes a review.

Attestation engagements

The Statements on Standards for Attestation Engagements (SSAE) apply when a practitioner reports on subject matter other than historical financial statements — internal control, sustainability metrics, compliance with a contract, prospective financial information. The three forms mirror the assurance continuum: an examination (reasonable assurance, opinion), a review (limited assurance), and agreed-upon procedures (findings, no opinion). All attestation engagements require independence and a responsible party that takes responsibility for the subject matter — the framework for the wide range of assurance services CPAs increasingly provide.

Issuers versus nonissuers

The standard-setter depends on the entity. Issuers (public companies) are audited under PCAOB standards, with the integrated audit and critical audit matters (CAMs) from AUD Unit 2. Nonissuers are audited under the AICPA's Statements on Auditing Standards (SAS / AU-C), which permit key audit matters (KAMs) only when engaged to report them. Recognizing whether an engagement is for an issuer or a nonissuer determines the entire body of standards that applies — a frequent exam trigger.

Governmental auditing and GAGAS

Audits of government entities and recipients of government funds follow Generally Accepted Government Auditing Standards (GAGAS) — the Yellow Book — which build on GAAS with added requirements: heightened independence (a conceptual-framework evaluation of nonaudit services), expanded reporting on internal control and compliance, and stricter continuing education. A GAGAS financial audit produces, in addition to the opinion, a report on internal control over financial reporting and on compliance with laws and regulations — reflecting the public-accountability purpose that distinguishes government auditing.

The Single Audit

An entity that expends $1,000,000 or more of federal awards in a year (the Uniform Guidance threshold effective for fiscal years beginning on or after October 1, 2024) must obtain a Single Audit — an organization-wide audit covering both the financial statements (under GAGAS) and compliance for major federal programs. Major programs are identified with a risk-based approach. The auditor reports an opinion on compliance for each major program and on internal control over compliance, and prepares a schedule of findings and questioned costs. Compliance audits generally follow AU-C 935.

Special-purpose and single-statement reports

Finally, the auditor may report on statements prepared under a special-purpose framework (AU-C 800) — cash basis, tax basis, regulatory basis, or contractual basis — which requires an emphasis-of-matter paragraph alerting users that the framework is not GAAP. The auditor may also report on a single financial statement or a specific element (AU-C 805). These tailored reports let a CPA serve users whose needs do not fit a full GAAP audit while still being transparent about the basis of presentation.

Prospective and pro forma information

CPAs also report on prospective financial information — forecasts (based on expected conditions) and projections (based on hypothetical "what-if" assumptions) — under the attestation standards. A forecast may be issued for general use, but a projection is restricted to specified users who understand its hypothetical basis. The practitioner can examine, perform agreed-upon procedures on, or (for internal use) compile the information, and every report emphasizes that prospective results may not be achieved. Pro forma information — showing the effect of a transaction as if it had occurred earlier — is examined or reviewed under a parallel framework.

Reporting on controls and the reach of attestation

The attestation framework reaches a growing range of subject matter. A practitioner may examine management's description of its internal control and the suitability of its design — the SOC 1/SOC 2 engagements from this unit's IT week, viewed from the service auditor's side. The same standards support assurance on sustainability and greenhouse-gas disclosures, compliance with contractual or regulatory requirements, and other emerging metrics. As stakeholders demand assurance beyond the financial statements, the SSAE framework gives the profession a consistent structure — subject matter, criteria, responsible party, and level of assurance — for whatever needs to be attested.

Restricted use and report tailoring

Many of these reports are restricted in use. Agreed-upon-procedures reports, projections, and reports on special-purpose frameworks intended for specific parties carry an alert paragraph limiting distribution to the users who understand the basis and the procedures. Matching the report to the engagement — its assurance level, its framework, and its intended users — is the final discipline of the AUD section: the same factual work can support very different reports. A report issued on the wrong basis, or distributed beyond its intended users, exposes the practitioner to liability even when the underlying work was sound.

CMA bridge

A privately held contractor like MBG more often needs a review or compilation for its lender than a full audit, and if it takes federal infrastructure money it could face a Single Audit. Knowing the assurance continuum lets the CFO commission the right engagement — and lets the auditor scope it correctly. This closes the AUD discipline that began with engagement acceptance in Unit 1.

Practice and recap

  1. Rank assurance: audit/examination (reasonable) > review (limited) > compilation/preparation (none); agreed-upon procedures report findings only.
  2. Apply SSARS (preparation: no report; compilation: report, no assurance; review: limited assurance, independence required) and SSAE attestation forms.
  3. Audit issuers under PCAOB (CAMs) and nonissuers under AICPA AU-C (KAMs only when engaged).
  4. Apply GAGAS (Yellow Book) added requirements and the Single Audit ($1,000,000 federal-award threshold; opinion on compliance for major programs).

Recap: engagements span an assurance continuum — audit/examination give reasonable assurance, review gives limited assurance, compilation/preparation give none, and agreed-upon procedures report only findings; SSARS governs preparation/compilation/review of nonissuer statements (review requires independence), SSAE governs attestation on other subject matter, issuers follow PCAOB and nonissuers follow AICPA standards, and government work adds GAGAS reporting on internal control and compliance plus a Single Audit when federal awards expended reach $1,000,000.

questions.explain: A review provides limited assurance via inquiry and analytics; an audit/examination gives reasonable assurance.

questions.q: Which SSARS engagement requires the accountant to be independent?
questions.explain: A review requires independence; preparation and compilation do not (compilation discloses a lack of independence).
